chunks: Muhammad ibn Ja'far al-Razzaz narrated to me from his uncle Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Khattab al-Zayyat, from Ali ibn Asbat, from Ismail ibn Mansur, from some of our companions, who said:

A servant of Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him) looked down at him while he was in his chamber, prostrating and weeping. He said to him, 'O my master, O Ali ibn al-Husayn! Is it not time for your grief to end?'

He raised his head toward him and said, 'Woe unto you! Or may your mother weep on you! By Allah, Jacob complained to his Lord of a matter much less than what I have seen, until he said, "Alas for Joseph, that he has lost a single son," whereas I saw my father and a group of my family slaughtered around me.'

And Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him) used to sympathize with the children of Aqil. So it was said to him, 'Why do you have more sympathy for these children of your uncle than for the family of Ja'far?' He replied, 'I remember their day with Abu Abdillah al-Husayn ibn Ali (peace be upon him), so I sympathize with them.'

key_terms.آلِ جَعْفَر: The family of Ja'far (Imam al-Baqir's lineage)
key_terms.يَوْمَهُمْ: Their day (referring to the day of Karbala/martyrdom)

ai.seo_question: Why did Imam Ali ibn al-Husayn show special sympathy to the children of Aqil?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Kamil al-Ziyarat* illustrates the profound, enduring grief of Imam Zayn al-Abidin (a.s.) by contrasting his collective mourning for his father and household with Prophet Jacob’s singular complaint over Joseph, thereby elevating the scale of Ahl al-Bayt’s suffering. It further elucidates the Imam’s specific affection for the children of Aqil, rooted in their shared participation in the Karbala tragedy, which deepened their spiritual bond through mutual loss. This narrative underscores the theological significance of *huzn* (grief) as a form of worship and remembrance (*dhikr*) within Shia tradition.
